name: RSI Mean Reversion

rsi_period.what: How many candles RSI looks back.
rsi_period.effect: Shorter = more reactive, more false signals. Longer = smoother, later entries.

rsi_buy.what: RSI level that counts as oversold and triggers the buy.
rsi_buy.effect: Lower = only extreme panics bought, fewer but better-bounce entries.

rsi_sell.what: RSI level that counts as overbought and triggers the sell.
rsi_sell.effect: Lower = exits earlier with profit locked in, but misses late legs.

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: Buy when the market is panicking (RSI below 30), sell when it's euphoric (RSI above 70). The classic 'fade the extremes' starter strategy.
idea: Prices whip back and forth around a fair value. When RSI drops below 30 the recent move has been unusually one-sided — and in a normal market, gravity pulls price back. This account buys the panic and exits the euphoria.
how: Compute RSI(14) on every closed candle.
RSI < 30 (oversold): buy with nearly all available cash (95% default).
Hold while RSI wanders between 30 and 70 — no fiddling.
RSI > 70 (overbought): sell the whole position.
No stop-loss, no take-profit: the RSI thresholds are the entire rulebook.
strengths: Simple, transparent, and easy to reason about.
Buys exactly when everyone else is scared — good entries in ranging markets.
Two parameters, no curve-fitting knobs.
weaknesses: In a strong downtrend it catches falling knives: oversold keeps getting more oversold.
Sells at RSI 70, which in a raging uptrend is far too early.
No trend filter — it fades trends as happily as it fades noise.
when: Works best when BTC is range-bound (chop between clear levels).
Suffers most in strong directional phases — both up (early exits) and down (early buys).
mistakes: Reading 'RSI 25' as a guaranteed bounce — it's a stretched rubber band, not a promise.
Loosening the sell threshold to 'let winners run' — that turns it into a different (trend) strategy.
Forgetting it's long-only: in a crash this account just buys the whole way down.
watch: Position badge: it should be long right after big red candles, flat right after big green ones.
Compare its curve with strategy 02 — one fades moves, the other chases them.

name: Dual EMA Crossover (9/21)

fast.effect: Smaller = crosses sooner with more whipsaws.

slow.what: The EMA that defines the prevailing mood.

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: The most famous trend signal in trading: when the fast EMA crosses above the slow one, buy; when it crosses back below, sell.
idea: A fast moving average represents today's mood, a slow one last month's. When the fast line overtakes the slow line, momentum has shifted up — the trend follower's cue to join.
how: Track EMA(9) (fast) and EMA(21) (slow) of closes.
Fast crosses ABOVE slow: buy with available cash.
Ride while fast stays above slow.
Fast crosses BELOW slow: sell everything.
Classic trend-following: late entries, no targets, exits only on trend reversal.
strengths: Captures the meat of sustained trends automatically.
Zero subjectivity — the rule either fired or it didn't.
Works on every timeframe and asset class.
weaknesses: Whipsaw hell in sideways markets: buy the cross, sell the cross, repeat at a loss.
Entries are late — you buy after the move already started.
The two EMAs are highly correlated, so 'two confirmations' is really one opinion.
when: Trending markets with follow-through (BTC trending phases).
Chop and tight ranges produce repeated small losses.
mistakes: Switching EMA lengths after losses ('optimizing' into curve-fitting).
Expecting it to call tops — it confirms trends, it doesn't predict them.
Judging it over a few trades; trend systems need many cycles to show their edge.
watch: Strategy state shows the EMA values each tick — you can see the gap widen in trends.
Pair mentally with strategy 01: when 01 loses, 02 usually wins (and vice versa).

name: MACD Signal Crossover

fast.effect: Smaller = more sensitive to short-term moves.

signal.what: Smoothing of the MACD line itself.
signal.effect: Smaller = signal crosses more often (more trades).

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: A momentum-change radar: MACD is the gap between fast and slow momentum, and crossing its signal line marks the turn.
idea: MACD subtracts a 26-period EMA from a 12-period one, so it rises while short-term momentum outruns long-term momentum. The 9-EMA signal line smooths it; their crossing is a cleaner, momentum-flavoured cousin of the EMA crossover.
how: Compute MACD line (12−26 EMAs), signal (9 EMA of MACD) and histogram.
Histogram turns positive (MACD crossed above signal): buy.
Hold while momentum stays with you.
Histogram turns negative (MACD crossed below signal): sell.
The histogram sign, not its size, drives decisions.
strengths: Combines trend and momentum in one number.
The signal cross filters out tiny meaningless momentum ripples.
Very widely followed — its signals attract real money.
weaknesses: Laggy: built on EMAs of EMAs, so turns arrive after price turned.
In flat markets the histogram saws around zero, whipsawing the account.
Doesn't distinguish strong vs weak trends (no ADX-style filter).
when: Moderate, persistent trends.
Bad in low-volatility chop and around major news reversals.
mistakes: Reading histogram HEIGHT as strength — this strategy only uses its sign.
Forgetting the defaults (12/26/9) are 1970s stock parameters, not BTC gospel.
Expecting early reversals; MACD confirms after the fact by design.
watch: State shows the histogram value with its sign — it flips only on crosses.
Long stretches of near-zero histogram = chop; expect whipsaws then.

name: Triple MA Trend (20/50/200)

fast.effect: Smaller = stack breaks sooner, both entries and exits.

mid.effect: The line whose breach triggers the exit.

slow.effect: Larger = more history needed, more stable regime filter.

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: The trend-stack strategy: only buy when SMA 20 > 50 > 200 — the whole market structure agrees the trend is up.
idea: One moving average is an opinion; three nested ones are a hierarchy. When the short sits above the medium above the long, every timeframe agrees: dips are being bought in an uptrend. When the 20 falls under the 50, the first layer of the stack has broken.
how: Compute SMA(20), SMA(50) and SMA(200) of closes.
All three aligned 20 > 50 > 200: buy (the full stack is bullish).
Stay long while the stack holds.
SMA20 drops below SMA50: sell — the stack's foundation cracked.
SMA200 needs 200 candles before this account can even think (warm-up 200).
strengths: Extremely robust: nested SMAs rarely give contradictory signals.
Stays in the biggest trends for a long time (the 20/50 breach is a late, strong exit).
A teachable model of 'multiple timeframe' thinking.
weaknesses: Very late entries and exits — gives back large parts of moves.
200-candle warm-up means ~2 days of 15m candles before first signal.
In a long bear, the stack never aligns and the account just sits in cash (fine, but idle).
when: Secular bull phases and strong recoveries.
Dead money in multi-month chop where the stack flips constantly.
mistakes: Using it to time exact bottoms — it buys AFTER the turn is confirmed.
Overriding exits because 'the 200 still looks fine' — the rule is the 20/50 break.
Comparing its flat bear-market curve to dip-buyers without noting it held cash.
watch: You can see the three averages in strategy state on aligned days.
Note how long it held during the last uptrend vs how quickly it exited.

name: Supertrend ATR Trailing Stop

atr_period.what: Lookback for the ATR that sizes the bands.
atr_period.effect: Shorter = stop hugs price tighter, exits sooner.

multiplier.what: How many ATRs the band sits from price.
multiplier.effect: Higher = wider stop, fewer shake-outs, bigger giveback. Lower = tigher, more whipsaws.

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: One ATR-scaled line that acts as trend and trailing stop at once: buy the flip up, ride until it flips down or the stop is hit.
idea: Supertrend draws a line at the price midpoint ± 3×ATR. While price stays above it, the line creeps up underneath — a trailing stop that breathes with volatility. When price closes through it, the whole regime has flipped.
how: Compute Supertrend from ATR(10) with a ×3 multiplier.
Direction flips from bearish to bullish: buy.
Hold; the Supertrend line is now your trailing stop, updated every candle.
Exit when price closes below the stop line or the line flips bearish.
Live state stores the stop and direction each tick.
strengths: A genuine trailing stop: winners run, losses get cut early.
ATR scaling means the stop adapts to BTC's changing mood.
Very few parameters, highly visual logic.
weaknesses: A single sharp candle against you can flip the line and exit at the worst spot.
In chop, stops are hit repeatedly — death by a thousand small losses.
No profit target: profits depend entirely on the trailing mechanism.
when: Clean trending phases with normal volatility.
Bad in whipsaw ranges and news-spike candles.
mistakes: Treating the flip as a prediction — it's a reaction to what already happened.
Tightening the multiplier to 2 'for less giveback' without expecting more exits.
Ignoring that gaps/spikes can blow through any stop — paper or real.
watch: State shows supertrend_stop and direction — compare stop to price each tick.
The stop should climb with price in trends and sit above price in falls.

name: ADX DMI Trend Strength

adx_min.what: Minimum ADX to accept a new long.
adx_min.effect: Higher = only powerful trends traded, far fewer signals.

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: Trend trading with a strength requirement: +DI over −DI is only tradeable when ADX proves the trend is actually strong.
idea: Most crossover systems fail because they trade weak trends. ADX/DMI separates the question: WHO leads (+DI vs −DI) and HOW STRONGLY (ADX). This account only buys when the bulls take the lead in a trend strong enough to be worth joining.
how: Compute ADX(14), +DI and −DI each candle.
Buy only when +DI crosses above −DI AND ADX ≥ 25 (strong trend, fresh direction).
Hold while +DI leads.
Sell when −DI takes over, or when ADX fades below 20 (the trend is dying of weakness).
The ADX fade-exit is the special sauce: it leaves before the turn completes.
strengths: Filters out the weak trends that kill naive crossovers.
Explicit strength-based exit (ADX fade) as well as direction-based.
Well-researched, institutional-grade indicator family.
weaknesses: ADX is slow — it confirms strength after the move is obvious.
Complex math, hard for beginners to debug by eye.
Strong trends eventually fade; the ADX exit can still give back profit.
when: Sustained directional markets with momentum.
Ranges produce few signals — ADX stays low and the account waits (correctly).
mistakes: Buying every +DI/−DI cross without checking ADX (that's the whole point of the filter).
Expecting ADX to predict — it measures what already is.
Using ADX < 25 as a sell signal — this bot only exits on ADX < 20 or direction flip.
watch: State prints ADX, +DI, −DI every tick — watch ADX climb during strong trends.
During calm chop ADX should hover low and the account should stay flat.

name: Ichimoku Cloud Breakout
entry: TK cross above the cloud, cloud green

kijun.effect: The mid-term anchor; its cross with Tenkan triggers exits.

displacement.what: How far the cloud is shifted forward.

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: The Japanese all-in-one system: price above the cloud with Tenkan over Kijun = buy; back inside the cloud or a failed cross = out.
idea: Ichimoku shows trend direction (the cloud), momentum (Tenkan/Kijun cross) and future support/resistance (the shifted cloud) in one picture. Trading it is trading a complete world-view rather than a single indicator.
how: Compute Tenkan(9), Kijun(26), and the cloud (Senkou A/B, shifted 26).
Buy when close is above the cloud TOP and Tenkan > Kijun.
Hold while the picture stays bullish.
Sell when close falls back below the cloud bottom, or Tenkan crosses below Kijun.
Inside the cloud = no man's land: the account never initiates there.
strengths: Combines trend, momentum and levels into one coherent system.
The cloud acts as a dynamic support/resistance map.
Very popular in crypto — its levels are self-watched by many traders.
weaknesses: Complex: 4+ parameters and several sub-signals to reconcile.
Slow: needs 80 candles warm-up and its signals lag.
Cloud computations with displacement are unintuitive to debug.
when: Clean trends where price travels outside the cloud.
Awful inside clouds and when the cloud is flat/overlapping.
mistakes: Buying a Tenkan/Kijun cross while price is INSIDE the cloud — this strategy refuses to.
Ignoring that a thick cloud is stronger resistance/support than a thin one.
Mixing Ichimoku timeframes (using daily settings on 15m bars without thought).
watch: State doesn't print the cloud — check the Market screen overlay when available.
It should be long during cloud-top rallies and flat inside clouds.

name: Parabolic SAR Flip

step.what: How fast the SAR accelerates per candle.
step.effect: Higher = stop chases price harder, exits sooner and more often.

maximum.effect: Higher cap = tighter end-of-trend stops; standard 0.2.

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: Pure trend-chasing dots: the SAR flip is both the entry signal and a stop that accelerates as the trend ages.
idea: Parabolic SAR dots sit under price in uptrends and above in downtrends, accelerating toward price the longer the trend runs. The flip is a complete 'trend changed' statement — this strategy buys flips and lets the dot do all exit thinking.
how: Compute SAR with step 0.02 and maximum 0.2.
SAR flips from above price to below: buy.
Hold while price stays above the SAR.
SAR flips back above price: sell — no second opinions.
The SAR effectively tightens each candle, so exits arrive faster as trends age.
strengths: Total objectivity: one dot decides everything.
Trailing behaviour protects profits as trends mature.
Very simple state to watch live (dot vs price).
weaknesses: Notorious whipsawing in sideways markets — dots flip constantly.
Acceleration means the exit can be very close to price in long trends (early shake-outs).
No consideration of volume or strength.
when: Long smooth trends — the SAR shines when direction persists.
Chop is its kryptonite.
mistakes: Using SAR as a top-caller; it flips only after price passes it.
Raising 'step' to 0.03 for tighter stops without expecting more whipsaws.
Forgetting warm-up 15: it needs a full SAR cycle to be meaningful.
watch: Live state holds the SAR value; compare its distance from price.
Distance shrinks as trends age — a sign the exit is approaching.

name: ROC Momentum Burst

period.effect: Shorter = fresher bursts, noisier; longer = smoother trend-ish momentum.

entry_pct.effect: Higher = only explosive moves traded (fewer, stronger entries).

exit_pct.what: Momentum level that ends the trade.
exit_pct.effect: At 0 it holds until the whole burst decays; above 0 locks profit earlier.

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: Momentum burst, measured bluntly: buy when price moved +2% over 12 candles and sell when that push fully decays.
idea: ROC is pure percentage change — no smoothing, no cleverness. A 12-candle ROC above +2% means a real push just happened; momentum traders bet pushes continue. When ROC falls back to 0%, the push is spent and this account leaves.
how: Compute ROC(12): % change of close vs 12 candles ago.
ROC ≥ +2%: buy (fresh momentum burst).
Ride while momentum persists.
ROC ≤ 0%: sell — the entire burst has been given back.
Exit at exactly zero: no profit target, momentum decay is the only exit.
strengths: Dead simple and transparent — one percentage.
Catches violent impulsive moves early (crypto's speciality).
Exit rule directly measures the bet ('momentum continues') failing.
weaknesses: Buys AFTER a 2% pop — vulnerable to buying local tops.
No trend context: a +2% bounce in a bear market also triggers it.
Zero-exit gives back everything if momentum decays slowly.
when: Volatile up-impulses (breakouts, short squeezes).
Slow grind markets never reach +2% in 12 candles — account sits idle.
mistakes: Assuming ROC predicts — it measures the recent past.
Treating the 2% default as sacred; it's just a parameter.
Expecting it to hold through pullbacks — the rule exits at exactly 0%.
watch: State shows ROC% — see it spike on green candles.
It should buy only after visible bursts, not during quiet climbs.

name: Aroon Trend

period.what: Lookback for counting candles since the last high/low.

strong.effect: Higher = only very recent highs qualify (higher conviction, fewer trades).

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: A freshness meter for highs and lows: buy when new highs are recent and dominant, sell when new lows take over.
idea: Aroon asks one question: how long ago did price make its highest/lowest point of the window? Aroon Up ≈ 100 means the high happened just now — the trend is young and alive. Stale extremes mean the trend died. Trading Aroon is trading trend-freshness instead of price.
how: Compute Aroon Up/Down over 25 candles.
Buy when Aroon Up crosses above Aroon Down while Up ≥ 70 (fresh high, new momentum).
Hold while Up leads.
Sell when Aroon Down crosses above Up.
Note: no strength filter on exit — any Down takeover ends the ride.
strengths: Measures trend age, which crossovers don't.
Clean, easy-to-read scale (0-100 both directions).
Catches trends while they're still young-ish.
weaknesses: In a fast pullback inside an uptrend, Down can take over and exit prematurely.
Reads only high/low recency — no price, no volume.
Whipsaws when highs/lows alternate rapidly.
when: Steady trends with periodic fresh extremes.
Bad in tight ranges where highs/lows alternate constantly.
mistakes: Buying whenever Up > 70 without the cross — the cross (takeover) is the trigger.
Thinking 100 means 'about to reverse' — it means 'just made a high'.
Ignoring that 25 is a short window: it's a tactical, not strategic, trend tool.
watch: State shows Up and Down — they should sit near 100 on fresh highs.
When both drop below 50, the market has no trend and the account should be flat.

name: Heikin-Ashi Trend

confirm_bars.what: How many clean bars must line up.
confirm_bars.effect: More = higher conviction, later entries/exits. Fewer = faster, noisier.

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: The no-wick trade: three clean Heikin-Ashi bullish bars in a row means relentless buying — buy the streak, sell the mirror.
idea: Heikin-Ashi candles average price into smooth blocks. A body-only bullish bar (no lower wick) means buyers never lost control all period. Three in a row is a streak of pure domination — the bot joins the streak and leaves when sellers produce their own three-bar streak.
how: Convert every candle to Heikin-Ashi form.
Wait for 3 consecutive bullish bars with NO lower wick: buy.
Hold while bullish structure continues.
3 consecutive bearish bars with no upper wick: sell.
Bar 3 of the bearish streak is the exit — it confirms sellers took over.
strengths: Beautifully visual — even a beginner can 'see' the signal on a chart.
The streak requirement filters single-bar noise.
Symmetrical entry/exit logic is easy to verify.
weaknesses: Smoothing hides raw price: HA bars lag reality by design.
3-bar streaks in quiet chop are common and fake.
No volume or volatility context.
when: Strong directional waves.
Chop creates short false streaks in both directions.
mistakes: Reading raw candles as Heikin-Ashi — the whole point is the transformed version.
Counting wicks on the body instead of open/low equality.
Expecting early exits; the 3-bar requirement means giving back some of the turn.
watch: Trades should cluster in waves — multiple trades per trend, not singles.
Flat during wick-heavy candles (normal pullbacks create wicks).

name: TRIX Signal Crossover

period.effect: Larger = even smoother, even slower, fewer signals.

signal.effect: Smaller = more crosses; larger = fewer, later.

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: Momentum so filtered it only sees the deepest swings: triple-smoothed EMA rate-of-change, traded on signal crosses.
idea: TRIX triple-smooths price (EMA of EMA of EMA), then measures that ultra-smooth line's rate of change. Every layer of smoothing strips noise; what remains is the market's deepest momentum pulse. Crossing its own signal line is a major, slow, reliable turn.
how: Compute TRIX(15): % change of triple-EMA.
Smooth it again into a 9-period signal line.
TRIX crosses ABOVE signal: buy.
Hold while TRIX leads.
TRIX crosses BELOW signal: sell.
strengths: Extremely robust against noise — trades only deep momentum shifts.
Near-zero false signals in normal chop (it simply doesn't fire).
A great study in what smoothing does to a signal.
weaknesses: Very late: entries can be far from the actual turn.
60-candle warm-up and heavy smoothing = slow account.
Triple EMA parameters are abstract — hard to reason about intuitively.
when: Long persistent trends.
Useless (but harmless — it stays flat) in chop.
mistakes: Expecting scalper behaviour from the bot's slowest momentum account.
Tuning period to 5 'for speed' — that defeats the triple-smoothing design.
Confusing TRIX units (% per candle of a smoothed line) with price %.
watch: Trades will be rare — that's correct behaviour.
Compare its entry quality vs strategy 02's on the same trends.

name: EMA Ribbon Consensus

periods.what: Comma-separated EMA lengths forming the ribbon.
periods.effect: More/faster EMAs = more sensitive; classic Fibonacci-ish spacing 8..55 balances speeds.

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: Five EMAs must agree: buy only the fully stacked bullish fan, sell only the fully stacked bearish one.
idea: The ribbon (8/13/21/34/55) shows trend at five speeds. When every line is ordered fast-to-slow from top to bottom, ALL timeframes agree — that's not a signal, that's a consensus. Tangled ribbons mean disagreement, and disagreement isn't tradeable.
how: Compute EMAs for 8, 13, 21, 34 and 55.
Fully ascending stack (8 > 13 > 21 > 34 > 55): buy.
Hold while the stack stays ordered (even briefly tangled? no — rule is exact).
Fully descending stack: sell.
Anything between (tangled): hold whatever you have, enter nothing.
strengths: The unanimity requirement produces very high-quality trend entries.
Transparent state: you can literally see the stack order each tick.
Naturally sits out tangled markets.
weaknesses: Slow: needs all five aligned, which happens late in trends.
One recalcitrant EMA (e.g. 55 lagging) blocks entries for a long time.
In strong trends it can exit on a single small bearish alignment then re-enter — chunky trades.
when: Textbook trends with orderly pullbacks.
Messy two-steps-forward-one-back markets keep it tangled (it waits, correctly).
mistakes: Reading 'most EMAs stacked' as the signal — the rule demands ALL five ordered.
Expecting entries near bottoms; unanimity arrives after confirmation.
Not noticing the exit is also a full alignment — half-hearted down moves don't exit it.
watch: State can show the five values — check ordering on trade days.
Ribbon tangles during pullbacks; that's normal and not an exit by itself.

name: Bollinger Bands Mean Reversion

mult.effect: 2 = ~95% of closes inside. Higher = rarer, more extreme touches.

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: The rubber-band trade: buy when price closes below the lower Bollinger band; sell when it snaps back to the middle.
idea: Bollinger bands wrap price in a statistically defined envelope. A close below the lower band means the fall is 2 standard deviations from the mean — unusually stretched. Rubber bands snap back; this account buys the stretch and exits at the mean (middle band), taking the statistical middle and leaving the tails.
how: Compute Bollinger(20, 2): middle SMA +/− 2 stdevs.
Close below the LOWER band: buy (stretched down).
Hold while price recovers toward the mean.
Close reaches the MIDDLE band: sell (reversion complete).
No stops, no targets — the bands define everything.
strengths: Statistical basis: touches beyond 2σ are genuinely unusual.
Self-scaling to volatility — bands widen in storms.
Objective exit (middle band) removes greed.
weaknesses: Trends ride the lower band for days — 'stretched' keeps stretching.
No trend/regime filter (strategy 41 fixes exactly this).
Sells at the mean, leaving the second half of bounces on the table.
when: Range markets with wide, honest swings.
Strong downtrends are its classic failure mode.
mistakes: Buying every lower-band touch in a crash (add strategy 40's gate mentally).
Expecting the upper band to matter — exits are at the middle band only.
Forgetting stdev on 20 candles is itself jumpy.
watch: Entries should be visible as closes poking below the lower band on the Market screen.
Exits at the middle band — quick round trips in healthy ranges.

name: Keltner Channel Breakout

mult.effect: 2 = two typical ranges beyond the EMA; higher = only huge expansions.

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: Volatility-expansion breakout: buy closes above the ATR-scaled upper Keltner band; exit when price falls back under the middle EMA.
idea: Keltner bands size their width with ATR, so the upper band marks 'price moved more than typical ranges allow' — a volatility expansion, not just a statistical stretch. When a close lands beyond it, real energy arrived. This account joins expansions and leaves when price re-enters the channel.
how: Compute Keltner(20, 2): middle EMA(20) +/− 2×ATR(20).
Close ABOVE the upper band: buy (genuine expansion).
Hold while price trades above the middle EMA.
Close falls back BELOW the middle EMA: sell.
strengths: ATR scaling reads the market's actual recent behaviour.
Catches real volatility expansions early.
Clean middle-band exit locks in the expansion's core.
weaknesses: Upper-band closes can be exhaustion spikes, not starts.
EMA middle exits early in strong trends (price rarely returns).
Category 'Mean Reversion & Channels' but behaves like a breakout account.
when: Volatility bursts after quiet periods.
Slow trends that never leave the channel produce nothing.
mistakes: Confusing it with Bollinger fades — same shape, opposite philosophy.
Expecting ATR and stdev bands to agree; they measure different things.
Buying wicks above the band — the rule is a CLOSE above.
watch: Entries should follow wide-range candles that exit the channel on the chart.
Compare its trades with strategy 06 — one buys the outside, the other the return.

name: Stochastic RSI Reversal

oversold.what: Zone where the buy cross must occur.

overbought.what: Zone where the sell cross must occur.

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: Extreme-of-the-extreme: buy when StochRSI %K turns back above %D while still below 20; sell the mirrored high-side cross.
idea: RSI can look oversold for weeks. StochRSI measures where RSI itself sits in its own range — sub-20 means RSI is at a short-term extreme even by RSI standards. Buying the %K/%D cross in that zone catches the exact turn of an extreme oscillator.
how: Compute StochRSI: RSI(14) → stochastic(14) → %K(3), %D = SMA(%K,3).
Buy when %K crosses ABOVE %D while %K was ≤ 20 (oversold turn).
Ride the oscillator recovery.
Sell when %K crosses BELOW %D while %K was ≥ 80.
strengths: Double-filtered extremes are rarer and more meaningful.
Cross-based entries avoid buying while the oscillator still falls.
Standard parameters, widely studied.
weaknesses: Layers of smoothing = late signals relative to raw price.
In strong trends StochRSI pins at extremes; crosses misfire or never come.
Four smoothing parameters are hard to reason about end-to-end.
when: Sharp but short-lived oversold spells.
Slow grinds keep StochRSI mid-range (few signals).
mistakes: Buying %K < 20 without the %D cross — the cross is the turn evidence.
Expecting RSI-level semantics; 20 here is extreme-for-RSI, not RSI=20.
Tuning only one of the four periods without the others.
watch: State shows %K and %D — entries should follow their sub-20 crossovers.
Check which candles produced the extreme: volume spikes make them more reliable.

EMA(50) confirmation means late entries near local tops sometimes.
when: Sustained trends with expanding peaks.
Chop: entries on weak crosses, exits on noise — small repeated losses.
mistakes: Reading the stop as a target — it's a maximum giveback, not a profit level.
Using daily ATR intuition on 15m candles.
Tightening the multiplier after one bad trade (whipsaw feedback loop).
watch: State stores chandelier_stop — it should climb with price during the ride.
Exits should come on the first close that undercuts a multi-candle peak.

name: Dynamic DCA (Dip Multiplier)

base_notional.effect: Higher = faster accumulation, faster cash burn.

dip_multiplier.effect: 2 = double down on dips; higher is more aggressive.

lookback_24h.what: Candles defining 'recent' for the dip test.

summary: The disciplined accumulator: buys every hour, twice as much when the last 24h is red — no timing judgement, ever.
idea: Nobody can time BTC. DCA doesn't try: it buys a fixed amount hourly, and doubles the order when the trailing 24 hours are down — buying the dip harder but still on a schedule. It builds a ladder of lots and never panics; optional take-profit exits the whole stack at a gain.
how: Every 4th candle (hourly): place a buy of the base notional.
If the trailing 24h (96 candles) is negative: double the order.
Skip if the order would exceed available cash.
Accumulate lots indefinitely (multi-position account).
Optional: if take_profit_pct is set, sell the whole stack when its average gain hits it.
strengths: Removes timing emotion completely — the strategy is a schedule.
Dip-doubling buys more when prices are cheaper.
No market judgement to get wrong.
weaknesses: In a long bear it keeps buying into falling prices (that's the plan — painful on paper).
Cash is finite: dips stop being doubled once affordable cash runs out.
Without a take-profit it can hold for years below average cost.
when: Always (it's time-based). Best in volatile-but-eventually-up markets.
Long secular bears stress it most.
mistakes: Judging it by win rate — DCA is about average cost, not per-trade hits.
Expecting it to sell rallies — by default it only buys.
Forgetting the dip-double still respects the cash constraint.
watch: Watch 'runs' in state — buys fire exactly every 4 ticks.
The 24h change in state explains why some orders were doubled.

name: Fixed-Step Arithmetic Grid

step_pct.effect: 1% steps must beat ~0.2% round-trip fees — smaller steps get fee-eaten.

levels_each_side.effect: More = deeper range coverage, more capital spread thin.

capital_pct.what: Equity share committed to the ladder.

reanchor_pct.what: Drift that triggers a ladder rebuild.
reanchor_pct.effect: Smaller = adapts faster, sells inventory more often.

summary: A machine that sells volatility: resting limit buys every 1% step down, each lot sold one step higher — round trips on autopilot.
idea: In a range, every dip is temporary. The grid places 5 buy orders below the current price and sells each filled lot exactly one step higher: a completed round trip banks the step profit (minus two fees). When price trends far away, the whole ladder re-anchors to the new location instead of holding dead inventory.
how: Anchor a ladder at the current price: 5 buy levels below, mirror levels above.
When price touches a buy level: fill it (limit order).
When price rises one step above a filled level: sell it — round trip banked.
If price drifts beyond the channel (6%): liquidate stale inventory and rebuild the ladder at the new price.
Levels are sized from current equity, so the grid shrinks after losses and compounds after wins.
strengths: Mechanically harvests range volatility — hundreds of small wins.
Re-anchoring keeps it alive through trends.
Beautiful live state: watch the ladder fill and sell in real time.
weaknesses: Each round trip nets ~0.8% after fees: trends give it no trips, only inventory.
Re-anchors lock in losses by liquidating underwater lots.
Range assumption can bleed slowly in one-way markets.
when: Chop between levels (BTC's favourite pastime).
Long one-way trends eat it via repeated re-anchor losses.
mistakes: Setting steps below ~0.4% — fees eat the whole edge.
Judging it on days without trips; grids earn in bursts.
Misreading re-anchor sells as strategy failure — they're the designed escape hatch.
watch: Live grid state: levels, round_trips, rebuilt count.
Round trips should accumulate during sideways sessions.

name: Martingale Dip Accumulator

dip_pct.what: Drop that triggers the next step.

multiplier.effect: 2 doubles; higher escalates faster toward the cap.

max_steps.effect: The cap IS the risk management — never remove it.

summary: The gambler's system, safety-capped: every 2% dip doubles the buy — up to 4 steps, and only while cash allows.
idea: Martingale logic: if you double each losing bet, one bounce recovers everything. Applied to dips: buy $100, price falls 2%, buy $200, falls again, buy $400... The cap (4 steps) and the cash check are what turn a blow-up machine into a (still spicy) system.
how: Anchor to the running peak price.
Price drops 2% from the anchor: buy the base notional.
Each further 2% drop: double the order (100 → 200 → 400 → 800).
Stop doubling at 4 steps or when the order exceeds available cash.
Optional take-profit sells the whole stack at a gain; otherwise it holds forever.
strengths: A single bounce fully recovers deep underwater positions.
The step cap and cash constraint bound the worst case.
Simple to understand and to watch.
weaknesses: Escalation is exponential: steps 3-4 dwarf step 1 in size.
In a sustained bear the cap forces it to stop buying exactly when things are cheapest.
Fees apply to every doubling — the ladder leaks 0.2% per round trip.
when: V-shaped dips in ranging markets.
Slow grinding bears break its heart (and its average cost).
mistakes: Raising max_steps 'for better recovery' — that's how martingales destroy accounts.
Judging it by unrealized losses mid-drawdown; the design is all-or-nothing-ish.
Forgetting every doubling must clear fees too.
watch: State shows steps and anchor_price — see the ladder build during dips.
The account should recover in one move when price bounces past the anchor.

name: Anti-Martingale Pyramid
entry: 20-candle high breakout, adds at each +2% leg

entry_lookback.what: Breakout window for the first leg.

add_pct.effect: Smaller = stacks faster in strong trends.

max_adds.effect: Higher = more compounding, bigger reversal risk.

trail_pct.effect: Tighter = protects more, exits on normal pullbacks.

size_pct.what: Leg size as share of starting balance.
size_pct.effect: Bigger legs = stronger compounding and losses.

summary: The winner's system: add a lot on every +2% leg of a winning breakout, protect everything with a 3% trail below the peak.
idea: If martingale doubles losers, anti-martingale adds to winners. Enter on a 20-candle high breakout, then each further 2% rise buys another leg (up to 3 adds, each 30% of starting balance). A 3% trail below the running peak exits the whole pyramid — so losses are always one leg, and winners can stack four.
how: Close breaks the 20-candle high: buy leg #1.
Each further +2% from the last add: buy another leg (max 3 adds).
Track the highest price since entry as the peak.
Price falls 3% below the peak: sell the entire stack.
Losing trades cost one leg; winners can compound four.
strengths: Asymmetric by construction: small routine losses, occasional stacked winners.
The trail converts 'let winners run' into an executable rule.
Multi-leg structure averages into trends at progressively better context.
weaknesses: A 3% pullback in a strong trend is normal — it will exit early sometimes.
Later legs buy near the top of the move if the trend is ending.
Stacked exposure means a sharp reversal hurts more than a single position.
when: Power trends with stair-step structure.
V-shaped reversals after the final add hurt most.
mistakes: Expecting every trade to pyramid — most will be single-leg exits.
Loosening the trail to 5% and forgetting giveback grows too.
Ignoring the add cap: unlimited adds = one reversal wipes many legs.
watch: State shows adds and peak_price — watch the ladder stack in trends.
Exits should come after the first 3% reversal from a visible peak.

name: Kelly Fraction Position Sizing

min_trades.what: Closed trades before Kelly is trusted.
min_trades.effect: Below this it trades the default 10% — small while learning.

max_fraction.what: Absolute cap on any Kelly bet.

kelly_fraction.what: Share of full Kelly to bet.
kelly_fraction.effect: 0.5 = half-Kelly: most of the growth, half the volatility.

summary: A breakout strategy whose position size is decided by mathematics: Kelly's formula from the account's own trade history — and it stands aside when the edge is negative.
idea: Most strategies decide WHEN to trade; Kelly decides HOW MUCH. This account enters Donchian(20) breakouts, then sizes the bet with the Kelly criterion estimated from its own closed trades: f* = p − (1−p)/b. No history (10 trades)? Trade small by default. Negative edge? Don't trade at all. The sizing is the intelligence.
how: Close breaks the 20-candle high: candidate entry.
Estimate p (win rate) and b (avg win / avg loss) from the account's closed trades.
Compute full Kelly, halve it, cap at 50% of cash.
Positive edge: buy sized to the fraction. No/negative edge: stand aside.
Exit when close breaks the 10-candle low.
strengths: Adaptive risk: sizes up only after the account proves an edge.
The negative-edge stand-aside is rare and brilliant.
Textbook link between trade stats and position sizing.
weaknesses: Kelly from 10-30 trades is statistically shaky.
In a small sample a lucky streak can justify huge sizes (cap helps).
Slow to adapt: estimates update only as trades close.
when: Long-horizon accounts where trade statistics can accumulate.
Early on it's tiny (default 10%) — patience required.
mistakes: Reading the Kelly fraction as a signal — it's a size, decided after the breakout.
Expecting full-Kelly growth; this account deliberately runs half.
Forgetting the stand-aside: no edge, no trade — that's a feature.
watch: State shows the current fraction and its p/b origin.
Watch the fraction grow after winning streaks and shrink (or zero) after losses.

name: Multi-Indicator Consensus Vote

threshold.effect: 3 of 5 = strict majority. Higher = rarer, more certain trades.

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: Five indicators vote, majority rules: buy at +3 of 5 bullish, sell at −3. Disagreement never gets traded.
idea: Every indicator has a blind spot — RSI lies in trends, EMAs whipsaw in chop. Instead of trusting one, this account polls five different toolboxes (RSI, EMA cross, MACD, Bollinger, StochRSI). Each casts ±1. When three or more agree, the trade has survived five independent worldviews.
how: Each candle, poll the five voters: RSI(14), EMA 9/21, MACD(12/26/9), Bollinger(20,2), StochRSI(14,14,3,3).
Each voter says bullish (+1), bearish (−1) or neutral (0).
Score ≥ +3: buy. Score ≤ −3: sell.
Scores between: no action — disagreement is information too.
The state prints every vote so you can audit the score.
strengths: Filters the whipsaws that plague single-indicator systems.
Auditable: every vote is recorded in live state.
Teaches exactly how indicators disagree — a free education.
weaknesses: The voters share inputs (all use closes) — less independent than they look.
Majority rule is slow: it needs most voters to flip.
In a crash all five vote bearish AFTER the fall — late by design.
when: Markets where half the indicators are right at a time.
Vicious trends where it arrives late but avoids false early entries.
mistakes: Adding more voters for 'safety' — correlated voters just double-count.
Expecting it to catch reversals early; consensus is a confirmation tool.
Ignoring the individual votes in state — they show WHY it traded.
watch: State prints all five votes + score — check the split before each trade.
Score ±1/±2 days with no trades are the strategy working as designed.

name: Trend + Pullback Confluence

mid_period.what: The trend-health line whose loss exits.

rsi_buy.effect: Lower = only deeper dips inside trends.

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: The two-layer trade: only buy RSI dips when the long-term trend (SMA200 > SMA50) says the market is still up.
idea: Naked RSI dip-buying catches falling knives in bear markets. This account fixes that with a gate: only buy weakness (RSI < 35) while price trades above the SMA200 with SMA50 above SMA200 — i.e., dips inside an uptrend. Selling requires RSI > 65 OR losing the SMA50. Trend and timing filters in series.
how: Trend gate: price above SMA200 AND SMA50 > SMA200 (long-term up).
Dip trigger: RSI(14) < 35 while the gate is open: buy.
Ride the recovery while the trend holds.
Exit when RSI > 65 (recovered) or price loses the SMA50.
strengths: The single best conceptual fix for dip-buying: context above trigger.
Buys in uptrends only — the exact opposite of catching knives.
Clear two-layer logic that generalizes to any strategy pair.
weaknesses: 200-candle warm-up and a strict gate = few signals.
A genuine trend break (price under SMA200) happens AFTER damage.
Two SMA filters are slower than one — exits lag.
when: Long uptrends with healthy pullbacks — its home turf.
Bear markets: gate closed, account idle in cash (correct).
mistakes: Buying RSI dips without the gate — that's just strategy 01 again.
Expecting it to short or fade the breakdown; it only holds cash.
Ignoring that 'price above SMA200' uses current price — a daily close below flips it.
watch: The gate state (trend up/down) should visibly close during corrections.
Entries should be rare and only after shallow dips in uptrends.

name: Volatility Regime Switcher

atr_period.what: ATR lookback for the regime meter.

high_vol.effect: Higher = only truly wild markets fade; lower = fades more often.

low_vol.effect: Lower = only deep compressions break out.

entry_period.what: Donchian high window in breakout mode.

exit_period.what: Donchian low window in breakout mode.

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: One account, two strategies, chosen by the market's mood: high volatility → fade with Bollinger; low volatility → break out with Donchian; in between → do nothing.
idea: Different market states demand different tools. When ATR sits in the top 30% of its own history, ranges are wide and mean reversion works — so it fades with Bollinger. In the bottom 30%, compression precedes breakouts — so it trades Donchian breaks. The middle 40% is noise: it sits out entirely.
how: Measure ATR(14)'s percentile rank over 100 candles.
Percentile ≥ 70 (high vol): switch to mean-reversion mode — buy closes below the Bollinger lower band, exit at the middle band.
Percentile ≤ 30 (low vol): switch to breakout mode — buy closes above the 20-candle Donchian high, exit below the 10-candle low.
30-70 (neutral): no trades at all.
State prints the current percentile and active regime.
strengths: Regime awareness is the future of systematic trading — this is its simplest honest form.
Both sub-strategies run only in the state where they're historically strong.
The neutral dead-zone prevents chop whipsaws by design.
weaknesses: Regime switches lag: by the time ATR percentile confirms, half the move is gone.
Two full sub-strategies to debug.
Percentile windows are fixed — regime 'normal' drifts over years.
when: Alternating volatile/quiet phases — it catches both.
In-between regimes: nothing (the 40% dead zone is deliberate).
mistakes: Expecting it to trade every day — the dead zone is the design.
Treating mode labels as predictions; they describe the last 100 candles.
Tuning high_vol/low_vol so the dead zone disappears — that's removing the filter.
watch: State shows ATR percentile and regime — see it flip after volatility bursts.
Fade-mode entries during wild candles, breakout-mode entries after quiet ones.

name: Sibling Performance Allocator

momentum_lookback.what: Reserved window for momentum measurement (kept for tuning).
momentum_lookback.effect: Not used by the current default logic — a placeholder for experimentation.

median_floor_pct.what: Median sibling return required to participate.
median_floor_pct.effect: 0 = trade while the median sibling is at break-even or better. Raise it to demand a healthier ensemble.

alloc.what: Share of the account's available cash spent on a single entry.
alloc.effect: None = the global default (95% of cash) applies. Lower it to trade smaller.

summary: The crowd-surfer meta-strategy: trade only while the median of the other 41 accounts is making money; ride the leader, stand aside in the slump.
idea: The ultimate regime filter is the bot itself: when the median sibling account is profitable, the market is tradeable; when the majority of 41 systems are underwater, it isn't. This account reads (never touches) its siblings' equity, participates while the ensemble median ≥ 0, and mirrors the best performer's behaviour.
how: Each tick, read the return of all 41 sibling accounts.
Compute the ensemble median return (and find the current leader).
Median ≥ 0: the market is tradeable — buy in.
Median < 0: the ensemble is bleeding — stand aside in cash.
State prints median, peer count and leader for full transparency.
strengths: A real ensemble/meta signal — 41 diverse strategies voting with their equity.
Completely mechanical market-health filter.
Deliberately documented exception to isolation, and read-only.
weaknesses: Correlated siblings (many trend accounts) make the median less diverse than it looks.
It participates when the median is fine but can still pick a bad moment.
Conceptually subtle — the hardest strategy in the zoo to explain quickly.
when: Any market — it adapts through the ensemble itself.
The ensemble is only as smart as its weakest correlated cluster.
mistakes: Judging it by its own curve — it's a meta-bet on the whole experiment.
Forgetting it does NOT copy the leader's trades; it rides 'participate/stand aside' only.
Reading its flat periods as failure — standing aside IS the strategy when the ensemble bleeds.
watch: State prints median_return_pct and leader — compare with the portfolio's total return.
It should be flat during portfolio-wide slumps and active during broad rallies.
